title: MTRX™ Field Guide to the Mind · Psychology and Philosophy · Weeks 1-2

cards.name: What is philosophy?
cards.q: True or false: philosophy is mostly personal opinions about the meaning of life.
cards.answer: False. Philosophy is about arguments: claims backed by reasons anyone can inspect and attack. Opinions are where it starts, not where it ends.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What is philosophy?
cards.q: Did physics and psychology start inside philosophy?
cards.answer: Both did. Newton's great book was called Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy (1687). Psychology left when Wundt opened his lab in 1879.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What is philosophy?
cards.q: In 60 words, explain to a smart 15-year-old what philosophy is and how it differs from science.
cards.answer: Philosophy works on questions we can't yet settle by measuring: what's real, what counts as knowing, what we ought to do. It answers with arguments that anyone can check and attack. Science grew out of it. Once a question gets a reliable method of measurement, it usually leaves philosophy and becomes its own field.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What is philosophy?
cards.q: Name philosophy's three big areas and the toolkit underneath.
cards.answer: Metaphysics (what's real), epistemology (how we know), value theory (ethics, politics, aesthetics), with logic as the shared toolkit.

cards.name: What is philosophy?
cards.q: Why do we only know Socrates second-hand?
cards.answer: He wrote nothing. We know him through Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes, mostly Plato.

cards.name: What is philosophy?
cards.q: What separates a philosophical position from an opinion?
cards.answer: A position comes with an argument that can be stated, tested and objected to. An opinion doesn't have to.

cards.name: What is philosophy?
cards.q: A cofounder says: "AI will replace all agencies within five years." Before you argue, what kind of question is it?
cards.answer: Mostly a factual prediction, hiding a definitions question: what counts as an "agency", and replacing which tasks? Pin down the definitions first, then ask what evidence would settle the prediction. Half of all business arguments are really definition fights.

cards.name: From skull bumps to science
cards.q: Is Freud's psychoanalysis the scientific foundation of modern psychology?
cards.answer: No. It shaped the vocabulary (the unconscious, defence mechanisms), but most of its specific claims are hard to test. The scientific core is experimental and statistical.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: From skull bumps to science
cards.q: What year is usually given as psychology's birthday?
cards.answer: 1879, when Wilhelm Wundt opened his experimental lab in Leipzig.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: From skull bumps to science
cards.q: In 60 words: what makes psychology a science rather than common sense?
cards.answer: It turns hunches into testable claims, measures behaviour carefully, compares conditions and checks whether results replicate. Common sense says both "opposites attract" and "birds of a feather flock together". Psychology asks which is true, for whom, and how big the effect really is.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: From skull bumps to science
cards.q: Why is 1879 psychology's birthday?
cards.answer: Wilhelm Wundt opened the first experimental psychology lab in Leipzig.

cards.name: From skull bumps to science
cards.q: What did the 2015 replication project find?
cards.answer: Of 100 studies, about 36% replicated with significant results (vs 97% originally), and effects were roughly half as large.

cards.name: From skull bumps to science
cards.q: What does WEIRD stand for, and why care?
cards.answer: Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic. Most classic findings come from such samples, so they may not transfer to other cultures.

cards.name: From skull bumps to science
cards.q: A LinkedIn post says: "Studies show people decide in 7 seconds whether to trust a website." What three questions does an insider ask?
cards.answer: Who were the participants, and how many? What exactly was measured (trust, or a quick rating of looks)? Has it replicated, and how big was the effect? Usually the answer is one small study, and the rating was of visual appeal.

cards.name: How to argue
cards.q: True or false: a valid argument always has a true conclusion.
cards.answer: False. Valid only means the shape works. "All fish fly; a salmon is a fish; so salmons fly" is perfectly valid and totally unsound.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How to argue
cards.q: Does "begging the question" mean "raising the question"?
cards.answer: Not in philosophy. It means circular reasoning: quietly assuming the very thing you're trying to prove.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How to argue
cards.q: In 60 words: the difference between valid and sound, with your own example.
cards.answer: Valid means the conclusion follows if the premises are true; it's about shape. Sound means valid and the premises really are true. "Every Ahmedabad clinic needs a website; Riya's is an Ahmedabad clinic; so it needs one" is valid, but unsound if the first premise is false.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How to argue
cards.q: Define a valid argument.
cards.answer: One where, if the premises were true, the conclusion could not be false. It's about form, not truth.

cards.name: How to argue
cards.q: What's a hidden premise, and why hunt for it?
cards.answer: An unstated assumption the argument needs. It's usually the weakest stone.

cards.name: How to argue
cards.q: What is steelmanning?
cards.answer: Restating the opposing view in its strongest form before you criticise it.

cards.name: How to argue
cards.q: Client: "Our competitor added a chatbot and they're growing fast, so we need a chatbot." Number the premises and find the weak one.
cards.answer: P1: the competitor added a chatbot. P2: the competitor is growing. Hidden P3: the chatbot caused the growth and would do the same for us. C: we need a chatbot. P3 is the weak stone, because it's correlation without evidence of cause. Ask what else changed for them.

cards.name: Real findings vs good stories
cards.q: Countries that eat more chocolate win more Nobel prizes (a real 2012 finding). Does chocolate make you smarter?
cards.answer: No. Rich countries buy more chocolate and fund more research. Wealth is the confound.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Real findings vs good stories
cards.q: What single feature lets an experiment show cause, not just correlation?
cards.answer: Random assignment to conditions. It spreads every hidden factor evenly across the groups.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Real findings vs good stories
cards.q: In 60 words: why correlation doesn't prove causation, using the chocolate and Nobel prizes example.
cards.answer: Chocolate eating and Nobel prizes rise together across countries, but a third factor, national wealth, drives both. Rich countries buy more chocolate and fund more science. To show cause you need an experiment that randomly assigns the supposed cause, so hidden factors like wealth get spread evenly.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Real findings vs good stories
cards.q: What is a confound?
cards.answer: A hidden third variable that causes both things you're comparing, making them look linked.

cards.name: Real findings vs good stories
cards.q: Why did Clever Hans seem to do maths?
cards.answer: He read tiny unconscious cues from questioners who knew the answer. Without a knowing questioner, he failed.

cards.name: Real findings vs good stories
cards.q: What does preregistration prevent?
cards.answer: Changing your hypothesis or analysis after seeing the data (p-hacking and HARKing).

cards.name: Real findings vs good stories
cards.q: Callers using the new script booked more discovery calls last week. Before you switch the whole team, what do you check?
cards.answer: Selection: did the better callers choose the new script? Randomly assign scripts across callers and leads for two weeks, decide in advance what counts as success, get enough calls per group, and watch for regression to the mean after one good week.

cards.name: Reasoning without certainty
cards.q: Is Sherlock Holmes's method mostly deduction?
cards.answer: No, it's mostly abduction: inferring the best explanation of the clues. Conan Doyle used the wrong word.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Reasoning without certainty
cards.q: The sun has risen every day in recorded history. Does that prove it will rise tomorrow?
cards.answer: Not logically. That's Hume's problem of induction. It's overwhelming inductive support, not proof.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Reasoning without certainty
cards.q: In 60 words: deduction vs induction vs abduction, with one example of each from your own work.
cards.answer: Deduction: every client pays a 50% deposit, Riya's a client, so Riya paid a deposit. That's certain if true. Induction: the last nine Instagram leads replied within a day, so the next probably will. Abduction: bookings suddenly hit zero, and a broken form best explains it, so check the form first.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Reasoning without certainty
cards.q: Which kind of reasoning guarantees its conclusion if the premises are true?
cards.answer: Deduction.

cards.name: Reasoning without certainty
cards.q: State Hume's problem of induction in one line.
cards.answer: Nothing logically guarantees the future will resemble the past, and any argument that it will uses induction itself.

cards.name: Reasoning without certainty
cards.q: Nyaya's smoke-and-fire example: what kind of inference is it closest to?
cards.answer: A careful induction or abduction backed by a general rule (wherever smoke, there's fire) and an example (the kitchen).

cards.name: Reasoning without certainty
cards.q: Website conversions dropped 40% overnight. Give three explanations, ranked, and the cheapest first test.
cards.answer: 1. Tracking broke (sudden and total drops usually mean measurement). 2. The form or payment step is failing. 3. A traffic mix change (ad paused, algorithm update). The cheapest test: did visits change, and does the tracking tag still fire? Rule out measurement before you rethink the marketing.

cards.name: Fast and slow thinking
cards.q: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much is the ball?
cards.answer: 5 cents, not 10. If the ball were 10 cents the bat would be $1.10 and the total $1.20. Your fast mind blurts "10" and your slow mind rarely checks.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Fast and slow thinking
cards.q: Are cognitive biases always irrational?
cards.answer: No. Many are smart shortcuts in their natural environment (Gigerenzer's "ecological rationality"). They misfire in unfamiliar or deliberately engineered situations.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Fast and slow thinking
cards.q: In 60 words: explain anchoring, and how you'd defend yourself against it in a price negotiation.
cards.answer: Anchoring means the first number you hear pulls your later estimate towards it, even if it's arbitrary. In a negotiation, the first price sets the playing field. Defend yourself by deciding your own number before the meeting, writing it down, and, when it's fair, naming your price first.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Fast and slow thinking
cards.q: Bat and ball: what's the answer, and why do most people miss it?
cards.answer: 5 cents. "10 cents" pops out of System 1, and System 2 doesn't bother to check.

cards.name: Fast and slow thinking
cards.q: Judging a startup by how much its founder looks like Steve Jobs: which heuristic?
cards.answer: Representativeness, ignoring the base rate that most startups fail regardless.

cards.name: Fast and slow thinking
cards.q: What did Kahneman admit about the priming research in his book?
cards.answer: That he'd placed too much faith in underpowered studies. Much of it failed to replicate.

cards.name: Fast and slow thinking
cards.q: You show three website packages: ₹15k, ₹35k and ₹75k. Which effect makes the middle one sell, and when is that honest?
cards.answer: Anchoring plus the compromise effect: people avoid extremes and pick the middle. It's honest if every tier is real and good value. It's manipulation if the top tier exists only as a fake anchor nobody is meant to buy.

cards.name: Science vs pseudoscience
cards.q: Can enough confirming evidence prove a scientific theory true?
cards.answer: On Popper's view, never. Theories can only be corroborated by surviving tests, or refuted.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Science vs pseudoscience
cards.q: Popper's favourite examples of pseudoscience were astrology and which two grand theories?
cards.answer: Freudian psychoanalysis and Marxist history as its followers practised it. Both could explain any outcome, so nothing could count against them.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Science vs pseudoscience
cards.q: In 60 words: what is falsifiability, and why does astrology fail it?
cards.answer: A claim is falsifiable if some possible observation would show it's wrong. Astrology's predictions are vague enough to fit almost any outcome, and failures get explained away ("Mercury was in retrograde"). Because nothing could ever count against it, it can't be tested, so it isn't science.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Science vs pseudoscience
cards.q: Why does one black swan matter more than a thousand white ones?
cards.answer: Confirmations can't prove a universal rule, but a single genuine counterexample refutes it.

cards.name: Science vs pseudoscience
cards.q: What is the Duhem-Quine point in one line?
cards.answer: You never test a hypothesis alone: a failed test might be blaming a background assumption instead.

cards.name: Science vs pseudoscience
cards.q: Name one famous finding that failed replication and one that held up.
cards.answer: Failed: power posing, ego depletion, social priming, the Stanford Prison Experiment as taught. Held: conditioning, anchoring, Asch-style conformity, CBT's effectiveness.

cards.name: Science vs pseudoscience
cards.q: A marketing guru says his funnel works for everyone, and when it fails it's because you didn't commit hard enough. What's wrong with that?
cards.answer: It's unfalsifiable through an ad hoc rescue: every failure gets blamed on you, so the method can never lose. Ask him what result would show his funnel doesn't work, and for numbers from people who failed, not just testimonials from winners.

cards.name: Science vs pseudoscience
cards.q: Week 1 boss fight (optional, 10 min). Take the claim "Two minutes of power posing raises testosterone and makes you take bolder risks" and run the whole week's toolkit on it.
cards.answer: Kind of claim: empirical and causal. Premises: posture changes hormones, hormones change risk-taking, so posture changes risk-taking. Evidence ladder: one small 2010 study (rung 4, no preregistration). Confounds: demand characteristics (participants guess the point), tiny samples. Falsification test: a larger replication (Ranehill et al., 2015) found no hormone or risk effect. Verdict: the headline claim failed. A small effect on how confident people say they feel may survive. Say it in the room: "Nice story, but the hormone effect didn't replicate."

cards.name: Your brain is guessing
cards.q: True or false: your eyes send the brain something like a live video feed.
cards.answer: False. The retina sends compressed, patchy signals. Each eye has a blind spot and only a thumbnail-sized patch of sharp vision. The brain fills in the rest so smoothly you never notice.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Your brain is guessing
cards.q: If you know an illusion is an illusion, do you stop seeing it?
cards.answer: Mostly no. In the Muller-Lyer illusion, knowing the two lines are equal doesn't make them look equal. Knowledge and perception run on partly separate tracks.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Your brain is guessing
cards.q: In 60 words: why is perception better described as a guess than a recording?
cards.answer: Your senses deliver patchy, noisy signals, so the brain combines them with expectations from memory and context to build its best guess of what's out there. Usually the guess is fast and excellent. Illusions, the Dress and the missed gorilla show the machinery at work: what you see depends on what you expect and where your attention points.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Your brain is guessing
cards.q: What's the difference between bottom-up and top-down processing?
cards.answer: Bottom-up builds perception from raw sensory signals. Top-down uses expectations, knowledge and context to interpret them.

cards.name: Your brain is guessing
cards.q: What did the invisible gorilla study show?
cards.answer: About half of people busy counting passes didn't notice a person in a gorilla suit. Attention limits what reaches awareness: inattentional blindness.

cards.name: Your brain is guessing
cards.q: What did Helmholtz call perception?
cards.answer: Unconscious inference: the brain infers the most likely cause of its sensory signals.

cards.name: Your brain is guessing
cards.q: You show a dental clinic owner two homepage mockups. He says the second one "looks cheaper", but it's the same layout with a different hero photo. What's going on, and how do you use it?
cards.answer: Top-down processing. The photo set his expectations (a perceptual set), and he read the rest of the page through that lens. Use it on purpose: the hero image and first headline prime how everything below gets judged, so test those first, not the footer.

cards.name: Could this all be fake?
cards.q: True or false: Descartes was a sceptic who believed we can't know anything.
cards.answer: False. He used doubt as a tool to find certainty, then argued (through God) that we can trust our clear and distinct ideas. He was trying to beat scepticism, not join it.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Could this all be fake?
cards.q: Can you prove, right now, that you're not dreaming?
cards.answer: Not conclusively, from the inside. That's Descartes' dreaming argument. Most philosophers reply by questioning whether knowing really requires that kind of proof.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Could this all be fake?
cards.q: In 60 words: what was Descartes doing with doubt, and what survived?
cards.answer: He doubted everything that could possibly be false: the senses (illusions), being awake (dreams), even maths (an evil deceiving demon). One thing survived: while doubting, he must be thinking, so he must exist. From that foundation he tried to rebuild knowledge, but his route back, through a God who doesn't deceive, convinces few philosophers today.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Could this all be fake?
cards.q: What are Descartes' three doubts, in order?
cards.answer: The senses sometimes deceive (illusions), you can't rule out dreaming, and an evil demon could fake even maths.

cards.name: Could this all be fake?
cards.q: What is the Cartesian circle?
cards.answer: Descartes uses clear and distinct ideas to prove God exists, then uses God to guarantee clear and distinct ideas. The argument goes in a circle.

cards.name: Could this all be fake?
cards.q: What is fallibilism?
cards.answer: The view that you can know things without being absolutely certain of them. It's the mainstream position in epistemology today.

cards.name: Could this all be fake?
cards.q: A security consultant pitches your client: "Your patient records could be hacked, so you need our five-lakh audit." How does Day 9 help?
cards.answer: Possibility isn't probability, the same move as answering the sceptic. Ask what the realistic threat is, how likely it is and what it would cost. Then match the defence to the risk. Descartes' method makes great threat modelling (imagine the worst deceiver) and a terrible buying rule.

cards.name: Meet the brain (it's not a map of boxes)
cards.q: True or false: we only use 10% of our brains.
cards.answer: False. Scans show activity across the whole brain over a day, and damage to almost any area causes problems. It's one of the oldest myths in psychology.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Meet the brain (it's not a map of boxes)
cards.q: Is the amygdala the brain's "fear centre"?
cards.answer: Only as a cartoon. It responds to lots of things that are important or surprising, including rewards, and fear involves many other regions too.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Meet the brain (it's not a map of boxes)
cards.q: In 60 words: what's wrong with saying "the amygdala is the brain's fear centre"?
cards.answer: It treats one region as doing one job. The amygdala is involved in fear, but also in reward, surprise and anything important, and fear needs other regions working with it. Brains work as distributed networks, and an fMRI "light-up" is a slow, indirect, averaged signal. "Involved in" is accurate. "Centre of" is a headline.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Meet the brain (it's not a map of boxes)
cards.q: Roughly how many neurons are in a human brain?
cards.answer: About 86 billion (Azevedo et al., 2009), not the old round 100 billion.

cards.name: Meet the brain (it's not a map of boxes)
cards.q: What does fMRI actually measure?
cards.answer: Changes in blood oxygen (the BOLD signal), a slow, indirect proxy for neural activity.

cards.name: Meet the brain (it's not a map of boxes)
cards.q: What is the "seductive allure" effect?
cards.answer: People find weak explanations more convincing when irrelevant neuroscience is added.

cards.name: Meet the brain (it's not a map of boxes)
cards.q: An agency pitches your client "neuromarketing websites proven to trigger the brain's buying centre". What do you ask?
cards.answer: Which study, how many people, and what was measured? There's no single buying centre. If the evidence is a lab scan of 20 people, an ordinary A/B test on real visitors tells you more. The neuro language is the seductive allure effect, used as a sales tool.

cards.name: When is a lucky guess not knowledge?
cards.q: True or false: if you believe something true and have a good reason for it, you know it.
cards.answer: That was the textbook view until 1963. Gettier showed cases where all three hold and it still isn't knowledge, because luck disconnects your reason from the truth.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: When is a lucky guess not knowledge?
cards.q: How long was Gettier's famous paper?
cards.answer: About three pages. It's one of the most cited short papers in philosophy, and he barely published anything else.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: When is a lucky guess not knowledge?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is a Gettier case, and why did it matter?
cards.answer: A Gettier case is a belief that is true and justified, yet true only by luck, so it doesn't count as knowledge. A stopped clock that happens to show the right time is the classic example. Gettier's 1963 paper broke the 2,000-year-old definition of knowledge as justified true belief, and no proposed fix is universally accepted.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: When is a lucky guess not knowledge?
cards.q: What are the three conditions in the classic definition of knowledge?
cards.answer: Belief, truth and justification: justified true belief.

cards.name: When is a lucky guess not knowledge?
cards.q: Give the stopped clock case in one sentence.
cards.answer: You read a stopped clock that happens to show the right time: your belief is true and justified, but only by luck.

cards.name: When is a lucky guess not knowledge?
cards.q: What does reliabilism say?
cards.answer: A belief counts as knowledge if a reliable process produced it (like good eyesight in good light), even if you can't spell out your reasons.

cards.name: When is a lucky guess not knowledge?
cards.q: Your callers booked 9 discovery calls on the day you changed their opening line. Do you know the new line works?
cards.answer: Not yet. That's Gettier-shaped: you might be right, but the evidence doesn't connect to the truth. A post-holiday Monday, one caller's warm list or plain chance could explain it. Run the new line for two weeks against the old one on the same lead segments. Then you'll know, not guess.

cards.name: Memory is a rebuild, not a replay
cards.q: True or false: a very confident eyewitness is probably accurate.
cards.answer: Partly false. Confidence at a first, fair identification carries real information (Wixted and Wells, 2017), but confidence grows with time, feedback and retelling. Mistaken eyewitness identification played a part in about 69% of US wrongful convictions later overturned by DNA.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Memory is a rebuild, not a replay
cards.q: Can you plant a memory of something that never happened?
cards.answer: In some people, yes. In Loftus's "lost in the mall" study (1995), about a quarter of participants came to remember, at least partly, a childhood event that never happened.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Memory is a rebuild, not a replay
cards.q: In 60 words: why can a confident memory be wrong?
cards.answer: Remembering isn't playback. You rebuild the event from fragments each time, and the rebuild can absorb later information, leading questions and retellings: the misinformation effect. Confidence grows with repetition, not accuracy. Loftus showed one word, "smashed" instead of "hit", raised speed estimates and planted broken glass. Treat vivid memories as reconstructions, especially old or often-told ones.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Memory is a rebuild, not a replay
cards.q: What did Loftus and Palmer change in 1974, and what happened?
cards.answer: The verb in the question, "smashed" vs "hit". "Smashed" raised speed estimates and produced more false memories of broken glass.

cards.name: Memory is a rebuild, not a replay
cards.q: What does the forgetting curve show?
cards.answer: Memory drops steeply soon after learning, then levels off. Spaced reviews flatten it.

cards.name: Memory is a rebuild, not a replay
cards.q: What did patient HM teach us?
cards.answer: Memory has separate systems: he couldn't form new explicit memories but could still learn motor skills implicitly.

cards.name: Memory is a rebuild, not a replay
cards.q: A caller says a dentist "definitely said call back Thursday at 4". The dentist says he never agreed. How do you stop this happening again?
cards.answer: Both memories are reconstructions, so don't play judge. Fix the record instead. Callers log the exact time and words in the sheet during the call, then send a WhatsApp confirmation straight after: "Confirming a 10-minute call with Kevin, Thursday 4 pm." A same-day written confirmation beats anyone's memory.

cards.name: Where does your mind live?
cards.q: True or false: most professional philosophers today are dualists, like Descartes.
cards.answer: False. In the 2020 PhilPapers Survey about 52% accepted or leaned towards physicalism, against 32% for non-physicalism. But that 32% is a big minority, not a fringe.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Where does your mind live?
cards.q: Did Descartes say where mind and body connect?
cards.answer: Yes: the pineal gland, a small structure deep in the brain. Neuroscience has found no seat of the soul there or anywhere else.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Where does your mind live?
cards.q: In 60 words: what's the mind-body problem, and what are the two main answers?
cards.answer: It asks how thoughts and feelings relate to the physical brain. Dualists like Descartes say the mind is a separate, non-physical thing, but then struggle to explain how it moves the body. Physicalists, the majority today, say the mind is what the brain does, but struggle to explain why brain activity feels like anything: Chalmers' hard problem.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Where does your mind live?
cards.q: What is the interaction problem?
cards.answer: If the mind is non-physical, how can it cause physical changes in the body? Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed it against Descartes.

cards.name: Where does your mind live?
cards.q: What does functionalism say, and why does it matter for AI?
cards.answer: A mental state is defined by its causal role, not its material, so in principle a mind could run on silicon.

cards.name: Where does your mind live?
cards.q: What's the hard problem of consciousness?
cards.answer: Explaining why physical processing comes with subjective experience at all, not just how the brain processes information.

cards.name: Where does your mind live?
cards.q: A dentist asks: "Does your AI receptionist actually understand my patients?" What's the honest insider answer?
cards.answer: Separate behaviour from understanding. "In the practical sense, yes: it books, answers FAQs and hands off in Gujarati and Hindi. Whether it understands like a person is an open question, so we built it to pass anything unusual to your staff." It's honest, and it sells better than overclaiming.

cards.name: What is it like to be you?
cards.q: True or false: you're aware of most of what your brain is processing.
cards.answer: False. Most processing never reaches awareness. Attention picks a small slice, and the brain smooths over the rest so well that you don't notice the gaps.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What is it like to be you?
cards.q: Have scientists found the brain's "consciousness centre"?
cards.answer: No. The leading theories disagree about where and how, and a head-to-head test of two of them didn't cleanly confirm either.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What is it like to be you?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is consciousness, and why is it so hard to study?
cards.answer: Consciousness is there being something it is like to be you: awareness of yourself and the world. Science can study its measurable side, such as attention, reports, sleep and brain correlates, but experience itself is only visible from the inside. Rival theories make different predictions, and a careful head-to-head test hasn't crowned a winner yet. Nagel's bat captures the gap.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What is it like to be you?
cards.q: What is Nagel's test for whether a creature is conscious?
cards.answer: There is something it is like to be that creature.

cards.name: What is it like to be you?
cards.q: What is blindsight?
cards.answer: Patients with visual cortex damage report seeing nothing, yet can locate objects far better than chance: processing without awareness.

cards.name: What is it like to be you?
cards.q: What was unusual about the Cogitate study?
cards.answer: It was an adversarial collaboration: rival theorists agreed predictions in advance. Neither theory came out cleanly confirmed.

cards.name: What is it like to be you?
cards.q: You're writing the AI receptionist's opening line. What does attention research say about the first five seconds of a call?
cards.answer: People filter hard, and only things they care about cut through, like their name or their problem (the cocktail party effect). Lead with that: "Hi, this is Smile Dental. I can book or move your appointment right now." Skip the long welcome. Attention is a narrow spotlight and you get one shot at it.

cards.name: What is it like to be you?
cards.q: Week 2 boss fight (optional, 10 min). A rival agency's pitch to your dental clients says: "Our AI receptionist truly understands your patients, remembers every caller, and never mishears." Run the whole week on it.
cards.answer: Perception (Day 8): speech recognition is a best guess too, so "never mishears" is false; Gujarati-English code-switching on a bad line will trip it. Scepticism (Day 9): ask for the error rate on real calls, not a demo. Brain (Day 10): "understands" at which level, word matching or the patient's actual need? Knowledge (Day 11): a correct booking from a lucky guess isn't reliability; ask how it handles ambiguity. Memory (Day 12): "remembers" means stored logs, which raises consent and data questions. Mind and consciousness (Days 13-14): it behaves as if it understands; nothing is experienced. Your counter-pitch: "Ours is honest about its limits: it handles 80% of routine calls and hands the rest to your front desk." Measure that 80% on your own pilot before you say it.

cards.name: Are you the same person you were at twelve?
cards.q: True or false: your body is made of exactly the same matter as when you were twelve.
cards.answer: False. Bodies change over time. That does not by itself settle identity: the philosophical issue is which kind of continuity matters, bodily, psychological, or something else.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Are you the same person you were at twelve?
cards.q: If a perfect copy of you wakes up, is it you?
cards.answer: Not straightforwardly. It may share your psychology, but if there are now two continuers, numerical identity cannot be one-to-two. Parfit uses branching cases to argue that identity may not be what matters.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Are you the same person you were at twelve?
cards.q: In 60 words: why does Parfit say identity may not be what matters?
cards.answer: Parfit imagines fission, where one person's psychology continues in two people. Numerical identity cannot branch, but memory, intention and character can continue in both. That suggests the thing we value is psychological continuity and connectedness, not a further soul-like fact of identity. The conclusion is unsettling but useful: responsibility and care can track relations.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Are you the same person you were at twelve?
cards.q: What is Locke's key shift?
cards.answer: He distinguishes the same person from the same body or substance and links personal identity to consciousness, especially memory and accountability.

cards.name: Are you the same person you were at twelve?
cards.q: What is the branching problem?
cards.answer: If one earlier person has two equally continuous successors, both cannot be numerically identical to that one person.

cards.name: Are you the same person you were at twelve?
cards.q: What does anatta deny?
cards.answer: A permanent, independent self or essence behind changing experience; it does not deny ordinary causal and ethical continuity.

cards.name: Are you the same person you were at twelve?
cards.q: A safari lodge wants a total rebrand. The owner says, "If the logo changes, it is no longer us." How do you frame the decision?
cards.answer: Ask what continuity matters to guests: the name, promises, service standards, local relationships, visual memory, or legal identity. Keep the psychological and contractual links that carry trust, then change what no longer serves the lodge. Identity is not a sacred logo; it is a pattern of continuity that can be redesigned deliberately.

cards.name: Can a questionnaire measure a personality?
cards.q: True or false: a personality test discovers five boxes inside your brain.
cards.answer: False. Traits are statistical summaries of patterns in responses and behaviour, not literal brain compartments. A score is an estimate with context, item wording and measurement error.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Can a questionnaire measure a personality?
cards.q: If a test is reliable, is it automatically valid?
cards.answer: No. A broken clock can be consistent. Reliability is necessary for many uses, but validity asks whether the score measures the intended trait and predicts something relevant.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Can a questionnaire measure a personality?
cards.q: In 60 words: why is MBTI weaker than a trait measure for serious decisions?
cards.answer: MBTI turns continuous preferences into categorical types, implying sharp boundaries that research does not support. McCrae and Costa found its indices were better understood as dimensions related to broader traits. It can start a reflective conversation, but a serious decision needs validated constructs, multiple observations, relevant criteria and humility about context and change.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Can a questionnaire measure a personality?
cards.q: Name the Big Five.
cards.answer: Openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism.

cards.name: Can a questionnaire measure a personality?
cards.q: What is the difference between reliability and validity?
cards.answer: Reliability is consistency. Validity is whether the score supports the intended interpretation and use.

cards.name: Can a questionnaire measure a personality?
cards.q: What does HEXACO add?
cards.answer: Honesty-humility, alongside emotionality, extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness to experience.

cards.name: Can a questionnaire measure a personality?
cards.q: One of your two commission callers scores “highly persuasive” on a quiz and asks for a higher commission. How do you respond?
cards.answer: Do not price a person from a label. Define the outcome, then inspect comparable evidence: qualified leads, show-up rate, conversion, revenue and client retention across enough calls. A personality score may suggest coaching questions, but it cannot replace behavioural data, a fair rubric and a trial period.

cards.name: Did your brain decide before you did?
cards.q: True or false: Libet showed that the brain makes every important decision before consciousness.
cards.answer: False. Libet studied simple, self-initiated movements and a reported urge time. The finding is relevant evidence, not a complete theory of deliberation, responsibility or long-term choice.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Did your brain decide before you did?
cards.q: If determinism is true, does punishment have no purpose?
cards.answer: No. A compatibilist can distinguish revenge from protection, deterrence, rehabilitation and fair accountability. A caused action can still reveal reasons, respond to evidence and be shaped by consequences.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Did your brain decide before you did?
cards.q: In 60 words: what does Schurger's model change?
cards.answer: Libet treated the readiness potential as evidence that unconscious motor preparation precedes conscious intention. Schurger, Sitt and Dehaene modelled the average buildup as the result of spontaneous fluctuations accumulating until a threshold is crossed. That can produce the same EEG shape without a settled unconscious decision. It weakens a headline argument, but does not prove metaphysical freedom.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Did your brain decide before you did?
cards.q: What is compatibilism?
cards.answer: The view that an action can be determined and still free when it flows from the person's reasons and desires without coercion.

cards.name: Did your brain decide before you did?
cards.q: What is the readiness potential?
cards.answer: An EEG potential that tends to precede self-initiated movement, especially in averaged data.

cards.name: Did your brain decide before you did?
cards.q: What did the 2020 PhilPapers Survey find?
cards.answer: Among 1,758 respondents, 59.16% accepted or leaned toward compatibilism, 18.83% libertarianism and 11.21% no free will.

cards.name: Did your brain decide before you did?
cards.q: A caller says, "The client rejected my proposal because the algorithm made them do it, so I have no responsibility for the copy." How do you answer?
cards.answer: The algorithm, prior habits and context are causes, not an automatic excuse. Ask whether the caller could inspect the evidence, respond to feedback and change the copy. Build that control into the workflow: show the metric, require a second look before sending, and record why the final choice was made. Responsibility grows with reason-responsive control.

cards.name: How does a notification train you?
cards.q: True or false: conditioning means the learner is passive and has no thoughts.
cards.answer: False. Classical and operant procedures reveal learning mechanisms, but attention, expectation, memory, goals and context also shape what is learned.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does a notification train you?
cards.q: If a reward stops, does a learned behaviour disappear immediately?
cards.answer: Usually not. Intermittent reinforcement can make behaviour persistent, and spontaneous recovery can bring an extinguished response back after a pause. Context and new learning matter.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does a notification train you?
cards.q: In 60 words: why can variable rewards be sticky?
cards.answer: A variable-ratio schedule makes the next reward unpredictable, so each response can still seem worth trying. The action is reinforced intermittently and often resists extinction. Phones are not identical to slot machines, but unpredictable messages can create a cue-check-reward loop. Add friction, predictable checking windows and a replacement reward to redesign the habit.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How does a notification train you?
cards.q: What is the difference between classical and operant conditioning?
cards.answer: Classical conditioning links a cue to a predicted event. Operant conditioning links a behaviour to consequences that change its future probability.

cards.name: How does a notification train you?
cards.q: What is a variable-ratio schedule?
cards.answer: A schedule that reinforces after an unpredictable number of responses, as in many gambling systems.

cards.name: How does a notification train you?
cards.q: What is extinction?
cards.answer: A decline in a learned response when the expected consequence no longer follows, although old learning can return in some contexts.

cards.name: How does a notification train you?
cards.q: Your safari-lodge client wants more direct bookings. The team proposes fake “only one room left” alerts and random discount pop-ups. What would you recommend?
cards.answer: Use ethical operant design: one clear booking action, transparent availability, a real price and a useful confirmation reward. Test page speed, copy and trust signals. Do not manufacture scarcity or variable discounts that train compulsive checking. Sustainable conversion comes from accurate cues and reliable value, not a conditioning trap that damages trust.

cards.name: The crowd is not a character
cards.q: True or false: the Stanford Prison Experiment cleanly proved that roles automatically turn decent people cruel.
cards.answer: False. It was influential, but the archive and later analyses found demand, instruction and selection problems. A role can matter without automatically dictating action.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: The crowd is not a character
cards.q: If a colleague misses a deadline, is blaming their personality always a fundamental attribution error?
cards.answer: No. Situations matter, but traits can matter too. The error is a bias toward dispositional explanations, not a rule that situations explain everything.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: The crowd is not a character
cards.q: In 60 words: what is the fair modern lesson of the Stanford Prison Experiment?
cards.answer: The fair lesson is not that roles automatically transform people. The experiment was methodologically compromised, and archive evidence suggests experimenters encouraged tough behaviour. Situations, identities and leaders can shape action, but people interpret situations and may resist. Treat the study as a warning about power and storytelling, not a clean proof of human nature.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: The crowd is not a character
cards.q: What did Le Texier's archive work add?
cards.answer: It documented demand characteristics, incomplete data, prior prison work, guard instructions, and weak immersion, using archives and interviews with 15 participants.

cards.name: The crowd is not a character
cards.q: What did the BBC Prison Study suggest?
cards.answer: Group identity and leadership shaped action. Participants first resisted hierarchy, and later a committed group built a harsher system.

cards.name: The crowd is not a character
cards.q: What did Morris and Peng find across cultures?
cards.answer: American participants and English-language newspapers leaned more toward dispositional explanations, while Chinese participants and Chinese-language newspapers gave more situational explanations for social events.

cards.name: The crowd is not a character
cards.q: A clinic client says a receptionist is lazy because she missed three calls during a software outage. How do you respond?
cards.answer: Separate the person from the system. Check staffing, call routing, outage logs, workload and training before judging character. If the pattern survives those checks, discuss performance. This is not excusing missed calls; it is preventing a costly attribution error and improving the process that a client actually pays you to fix.

cards.name: The group can lend you a mind
cards.q: True or false: Asch showed that almost everyone conforms when a group is unanimous.
cards.answer: False. The classic data contain substantial independence. In a 2023 replication, the standard line-task error rate was 33 percent, and monetary incentives reduced it to 25 percent, but influence remained.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: The group can lend you a mind
cards.q: Does Milgram show that people obey blindly?
cards.answer: Not necessarily. Haslam and Reicher argue that many participants were engaged followers who identified with the scientific project and saw continuing as worthwhile. Distress and resistance were part of the record.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: The group can lend you a mind
cards.q: In 60 words: how can social influence be powerful without being automatic?
cards.answer: People use groups as evidence and as social belonging. A unanimous crowd can make an obvious answer feel socially costly, while an admired leader can make harmful work feel morally valuable. Yet Asch found many independent answers, Milgram recorded resistance, and minorities can introduce new frames. Influence changes probabilities; it does not erase agency.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: The group can lend you a mind
cards.q: What did Asch actually find?
cards.answer: A substantial minority conformed, but most critical responses were independent. A 2023 replication found a 33 percent error rate, reduced to 25 percent with incentives.

cards.name: The group can lend you a mind
cards.q: What is engaged followership?
cards.answer: People actively identify with a leader or cause and carry out actions they believe serve a worthwhile collective goal, rather than obeying mindlessly.

cards.name: The group can lend you a mind
cards.q: What are groupthink and polarisation?
cards.answer: Groupthink is suppressed critical evaluation under pressure for unanimity. Polarisation is a shift toward a more extreme version of a group's initial average after discussion.

cards.name: The group can lend you a mind
cards.q: Your startup team is choosing a launch date. The founder loves a festival-week launch, everyone nods, and the dissenting developer stays quiet. What do you change?
cards.answer: Separate idea generation from decision, ask each person for a private forecast before the meeting, appoint a red-team owner, and record the strongest objection. Then compare the launch against base rates, staffing and client risk. The goal is not permanent dissent; it is making disagreement safe before the group drifts into groupthink.

cards.name: Belief is a social act
cards.q: True or false: a conspiracy theory is simply any claim that two people secretly planned something.
cards.answer: False. Ordinary conspiracies happen. In this research tradition, a conspiracy theory explains significant events through a hidden, powerful and usually malevolent group, often with speculative and self-sealing features.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Belief is a social act
cards.q: Does epistemic responsibility require certainty before any action?
cards.answer: No. It requires proportion: inspect evidence, disclose uncertainty, seek correction and choose reversible, low-harm actions where confidence is limited.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Belief is a social act
cards.q: In 60 words: what is epistemic responsibility when evidence is incomplete?
cards.answer: It is not waiting for certainty or believing whatever feels useful. It is matching confidence to evidence, checking source and message, looking for disconfirmation, naming uncertainty, and choosing proportionate action. Because beliefs travel through groups, repeating a claim can impose costs on others. A responsible person stays corrigible, especially when identity makes a story satisfying.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Belief is a social act
cards.q: What three motives organise much conspiracy belief research?
cards.answer: Epistemic motives for understanding, existential motives for control and security, and social motives for a positive image of self or group.

cards.name: Belief is a social act
cards.q: What is Clifford's central warning?
cards.answer: Belief on insufficient evidence is ethically dangerous because beliefs influence conduct and testimony, so the duty is to inquire responsibly.

cards.name: Belief is a social act
cards.q: What does epistemic vigilance check?
cards.answer: It checks the content of a message and the reliability, incentives and trustworthiness of its source.

cards.name: Belief is a social act
cards.q: A new AI vendor tells you a rival agency secretly manipulates search rankings, and offers your studio a rushed six-month contract to fight it. How do you proceed?
cards.answer: Separate the allegation from the contract. Ask for independently verifiable data, alternative explanations, a test that could disconfirm the claim, and the vendor's incentives. Do not repeat the accusation as fact. If a small audit is justified, make it bounded and reversible. Responsible scepticism protects your reputation without pretending hidden coordination is impossible.

cards.name: Belief is a social act
cards.q: A brilliant developer joins a high-commitment, cult-like startup. The founder says outsiders are jealous, critics are agents of the old industry, twelve-hour work proves moral seriousness, and every setback proves the team is close to breakthrough. Analyse why a smart person might join and stay, using the whole week. Then propose a responsible intervention that protects the person without humiliating them.
cards.answer: Model answer: Day 15: the startup offers a new identity, a heroic story that makes work feel like a self. Day 16: a founder may over-read personality tests and label loyalty as character, while the developer may use intelligence as evidence that their judgement cannot be captured. Day 17: causes and pressures constrain choice, but responsibility remains in the next decision and in designing exits. Day 18: praise, equity promises and intermittent wins condition overwork. Day 19: do not call the developer irrational; inspect the founder's setting, power and identity leadership. Day 20: conformity, engaged followership, groupthink and polarisation make dissent costly, while a consistent minority can reopen a question. Day 21: conspiracy stories satisfy needs for certainty, control and belonging, but epistemic vigilance asks for sources, disconfirmation and proportionate action. Intervene privately: keep the relationship, ask what evidence could change their mind, map hours, health and financial risk, speak with a trusted outsider, and create a reversible exit plan. No ridicule, no counter-cult certainty. The aim is agency plus evidence, not winning a debate.

cards.name: Your face is not a mood meter
cards.q: True or false: a racing heart is a reliable sign of fear.
cards.answer: False. A racing heart also occurs during excitement, exercise, anger, illness and anticipation. The body signal is underdetermined, so context and interpretation matter.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Your face is not a mood meter
cards.q: If someone smiles, do you know they are happy?
cards.answer: No. Smiles can signal amusement, politeness, embarrassment, appeasement or social coordination. A face is evidence about an interaction, not a transparent window into a feeling.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Your face is not a mood meter
cards.q: In 60 words: why is a face not a reliable emotion meter?
cards.answer: A facial movement is an observable action, not a private emotion label. The same smile or tense brow can fit several situations, and people learn emotion concepts through language and culture. Body state, context, voice, history and the person's own report improve the inference. Ask before you conclude.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Your face is not a mood meter
cards.q: What does James-Lange put first?
cards.answer: A stimulus produces bodily changes, and the felt perception of those changes is the emotion.

cards.name: Your face is not a mood meter
cards.q: What are Schachter and Singer's two factors?
cards.answer: Physiological arousal and a cognitive interpretation of what that arousal means in context.

cards.name: Your face is not a mood meter
cards.q: What did the Himba study challenge?
cards.answer: It challenged the idea that posed facial expressions have universally recognised emotion meanings independent of concepts and context.

cards.name: Your face is not a mood meter
cards.q: A safari lodge client says your new price page feels aggressive because one team member looks tense in a review call. How do you respond?
cards.answer: Do not accept either reading as a fact. Ask what in the page or call produced that impression, check the words and the context, and invite the teammate to say what they meant. Emotion science supports a testable conversation, not a facial lie detector.

cards.name: Are moral truths out there?
cards.q: True or false: anti-realism means that people cannot have moral reasons.
cards.answer: False. Anti-realists can defend reasons as constructed, prudential, contractual or expressive. The debate is about what makes a moral claim true, not whether people can deliberate.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Are moral truths out there?
cards.q: If a culture approves an act, is it automatically right according to relativism?
cards.answer: Not automatically. Relativist theories differ about whose norms count, how internal disagreement works and whether criticism across cultures is possible. Relativism is a family, not one permission slip.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Are moral truths out there?
cards.q: In 60 words: distinguish realism, error theory and expressivism.
cards.answer: Realism says some moral claims are true independently of our attitudes. Error theory agrees that ordinary moral claims aim at objective truth but says they are all false because the required facts do not exist. Expressivism says moral language primarily expresses commitments or attitudes and guides action rather than reporting stance-independent facts.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Are moral truths out there?
cards.q: What does metaethics ask?
cards.answer: It asks what moral claims mean, whether moral facts exist, and how moral knowledge or motivation could work.

cards.name: Are moral truths out there?
cards.q: What is Mackie's error theory?
cards.answer: Moral claims purport to report objective facts, but no such facts exist, so ordinary moral claims are systematically in error.

cards.name: Are moral truths out there?
cards.q: Name Haidt's original five foundations.
cards.answer: Care or harm, fairness or reciprocity, loyalty, authority and purity or sanctity.

cards.name: Are moral truths out there?
cards.q: A client wants callers paid commission only when a lead closes, even if the caller did honest qualification work. How do you make the disagreement productive?
cards.answer: Separate the levels. At the normative level, compare fairness, incentives and consequences. At the metaethical level, notice whether the team treats fairness as a shared rule, an expression of respect or a fact that should bind everyone. Then write a transparent policy and test its effects rather than hiding a value choice inside a spreadsheet.

cards.name: Kant and the rule you would give everyone
cards.q: True or false: Kant says moral action is whatever produces the best outcome.
cards.answer: False. Kant makes the principle and the respect shown to rational agents central. Outcomes matter to ordinary judgement, but they do not define the moral law.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Kant and the rule you would give everyone
cards.q: Does universalising a maxim mean asking whether everyone doing the same thing would have good consequences?
cards.answer: Not exactly. Kant asks whether the maxim can be conceived and willed as a universal law without contradiction. That is a test of principle and agency, not a simple forecast of totals.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Kant and the rule you would give everyone
cards.q: In 60 words: how does the categorical imperative test an action?
cards.answer: State the action as a maxim, including the purpose that makes it intelligible. Ask whether you could conceive and will that maxim as a universal law. Then check whether the action respects every person as an end rather than merely using them. The test targets principles of agency, not a quick count of consequences.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Kant and the rule you would give everyone
cards.q: What is a maxim?
cards.answer: The practical principle or policy a person acts on, including the purpose that makes the action intelligible.

cards.name: Kant and the rule you would give everyone
cards.q: Name Kant's three formulations used here.
cards.answer: Universal law, humanity as an end, and the kingdom of ends.

cards.name: Kant and the rule you would give everyone
cards.q: What is nishkama karma?
cards.answer: Action done as duty without attachment to the fruits or results, while avoiding the opposite error of inaction.

cards.name: Kant and the rule you would give everyone
cards.q: A client asks you to hide a known limitation in a clinic website until after payment. What would Kant ask, and what should you do?
cards.answer: State the maxim: I will conceal material information when disclosure threatens a sale. Universalising it destroys honest consent, and it treats the client and patients as means. Disclose the limitation in plain language, document the decision and offer a remedy. A short-term conversion win is not a licence to use people.

cards.name: Can the numbers decide?
cards.q: True or false: utilitarianism means doing whatever feels kindest to the person nearest you.
cards.answer: False. It counts the wellbeing of everyone affected, including strangers and future people. Distance and emotional vividness are not moral weights in the theory.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Can the numbers decide?
cards.q: Does the trolley problem prove that people are secretly utilitarians?
cards.answer: No. Trolley answers reveal patterns in judgement under a narrow prompt. They do not by themselves identify a moral theory, and real policy involves uncertainty, institutions and trust.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Can the numbers decide?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is the strongest utilitarian case for and against using it at work?
cards.answer: The case for it is impartiality: count clients, staff, callers and strangers rather than privileging the loudest person, then compare expected benefits and harms. The case against simple maximisation is that rights, trust, uncertainty and distribution can disappear inside one total. Use consequence analysis with explicit constraints and transparent assumptions.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Can the numbers decide?
cards.q: What is Bentham's hedonic calculus for?
cards.answer: It is a proposed way to compare pleasures and pains by dimensions such as intensity, duration, certainty and extent.

cards.name: Can the numbers decide?
cards.q: How does Mill modify Bentham?
cards.answer: Mill argues that pleasures differ in quality as well as quantity, with competent judges preferring some higher intellectual and moral pleasures.

cards.name: Can the numbers decide?
cards.q: What did the Moral Machine experiment collect?
cards.answer: It gathered 40 million online decisions from millions of people across 233 countries and territories about autonomous-vehicle dilemmas.

cards.name: Can the numbers decide?
cards.q: You can raise prices by 8 percent with a hidden renewal clause, or explain the full cost and accept slower growth. What would a serious utilitarian analysis do?
cards.answer: Count immediate revenue, client affordability, support load, caller commissions, churn, referrals and long-run trust. Include the risk that the hidden clause harms people who miss it. If transparent pricing produces less short-term utility but protects many clients and the firm's reliability, it may be the better outcome. In any case, do not hide the assumption or call one metric morality.

cards.name: Character is what practice makes
cards.q: True or false: Aristotle means virtue is always the average between two equal amounts.
cards.answer: False. The mean is not a numerical midpoint. The right response depends on the person, stakes and situation: courage is not half-way between fear and recklessness, and some actions, such as cruelty, have no virtuous middle.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Character is what practice makes
cards.q: Can a good person flourish with no friends, resources or opportunities?
cards.answer: Not fully, on Aristotle's account. Virtue is central, but severe deprivation can remove the opportunities for virtuous activity. That dependence on external goods is one of the view's attractive and troubling features.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Character is what practice makes
cards.q: In 60 words: why is Aristotle's golden mean not a call to split the difference?
cards.answer: The mean is a fitting response relative to the situation, not a numerical midpoint. Courage can require a dangerous act, while recklessness is excessive and cowardice deficient. Practical wisdom reads the stakes, motives and people involved. Repeatedly choosing that fitting response builds a character disposition, so future choices become easier and more reliable.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Character is what practice makes
cards.q: What does eudaimonia mean for Aristotle?
cards.answer: Flourishing: excellent rational activity across a whole life, not a temporary feeling of pleasure.

cards.name: Character is what practice makes
cards.q: What does phronesis add to a rule?
cards.answer: Practical wisdom judges what the situation calls for, including when and how a general virtue applies.

cards.name: Character is what practice makes
cards.q: How does VIA differ from Aristotle?
cards.answer: VIA operationalises proposed character strengths in psychological measures. It can provide data, but its categories and six-virtue structure remain debated and do not replace practical wisdom.

cards.name: Character is what practice makes
cards.q: You are deciding whether to accept a lucrative wildlife client whose campaign would exaggerate conservation results. What would Aristotle and Confucius ask you to practise?
cards.answer: Aristotle would ask which character the deal rehearses, then use phronesis to balance courage, honesty, loyalty and the real consequences. Confucius would add role and relationship: what does a trustworthy junzi owe clients, staff and the public? A good answer may be a candid counter-proposal, not a heroic refusal or a quiet lie.

cards.name: Freedom when the script is gone
cards.q: True or false: existentialism says nothing has meaning, so any choice is equally good.
cards.answer: False. Existentialists reject a ready-made guarantee of meaning, but they still discuss responsibility, commitment, authenticity and the freedom of others. Camus answers the absurd with lucid revolt, not with a permission slip for cruelty.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Freedom when the script is gone
cards.q: Is Camus an existentialist?
cards.answer: He is routinely grouped with existentialists, but he rejected the label and developed absurdism in a distinct direction. He shared the questions of freedom, death and meaning while disagreeing with Sartre and with some existentialist conclusions.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Freedom when the script is gone
cards.q: In 60 words: what is Sartre's bad faith?
cards.answer: Bad faith is self-deception about freedom. Someone treats a role, job title or social script as a fixed essence, or pretends that freedom means having no constraints. Sartre's point is not that circumstances are unreal. It is that we still interpret and answer them, so saying the role made the choice can hide responsibility.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Freedom when the script is gone
cards.q: How is absurdism different from existentialism?
cards.answer: Camus's absurdism names the clash between our demand for meaning and an indifferent world, then recommends lucid revolt. Existentialism is a broader, diverse family about existence, freedom, responsibility and meaning.

cards.name: Freedom when the script is gone
cards.q: What is bad faith?
cards.answer: A way of hiding one's situated freedom by treating a role, excuse or circumstance as a fixed essence that removes responsibility.

cards.name: Freedom when the script is gone
cards.q: What is the honest claim about Frankl's camps?
cards.answer: He was imprisoned in four camps from 1942 to 1945 and later interpreted survival through meaning. His prewar logotherapy predates the camps, and his story cannot be turned into a universal promise that meaning defeats oppression.

cards.name: Freedom when the script is gone
cards.q: A client asks you to make a wildlife resort look sustainable while hiding its water use. You want the money and the director credit. How would the four thinkers sharpen the decision?
cards.answer: Kierkegaard asks what commitment you can inwardly own, not merely explain. Sartre asks whether you are hiding behind the agency role. Beauvoir asks what your choice enables or denies for workers, visitors and local communities. Camus asks you to face the ugly facts without a comforting story. The honest move is to offer a truthful redesign or decline.

cards.name: A good life is more than a good feeling
cards.q: True or false: the experience machine proves that pleasure is not part of a good life.
cards.answer: False. Nozick challenges the idea that pleasure is all that matters. His thought experiment does not show that pleasure is worthless, and later studies find that people's responses change with framing and with less invasive interventions.

cards.name: A good life is more than a good feeling
cards.q: Why did the famous income result use about 75,000 dollars?
cards.answer: That was the approximate midpoint of a 60,000 to 90,000 dollar income category in the 2010 study, not a universal biological threshold. Later work found different patterns, and the 2023 collaboration reconciled much of the disagreement.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: A good life is more than a good feeling
cards.q: In 60 words: why is a good life not reducible to happiness in the moment?
cards.answer: Momentary happiness matters, but a life can also be judged by what its person does, becomes and sustains. Nozick's machine tests whether pleasure alone is enough. Ryff adds purpose, growth, autonomy, mastery, self-acceptance and relationships. A credible good-life plan therefore tracks feelings alongside agency, meaning, health, relationships and ethical responsibility.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: A good life is more than a good feeling
cards.q: What is the hedonic versus eudaimonic distinction?
cards.answer: Hedonic well-being concerns pleasure and feeling good. Eudaimonic well-being concerns functioning and flourishing through purpose, growth, relationships, agency and virtue.

cards.name: A good life is more than a good feeling
cards.q: What did the 2023 income collaboration find?
cards.answer: The average linear rise and the flattening result can both appear: flattening is concentrated among the least happy roughly 15 to 20 percent, while happier groups keep rising or accelerate. The overall income association is real but weak.

cards.name: A good life is more than a good feeling
cards.q: Name two of Ryff's six dimensions.
cards.answer: Any two of self-acceptance, positive relations, autonomy, environmental mastery, purpose in life and personal growth.

cards.name: A good life is more than a good feeling
cards.q: You want enough MTRX income to travel as a nomad, enough time to write, and eventually the stamina to direct a film. How do you stop a bigger revenue number from silently becoming your definition of success?
cards.answer: Write a dashboard with four columns: experienced well-being, eudaimonic work, relationships and ethics. Track sleep and delight, hours writing or directing, time with people who matter, and whether client work is truthful and useful. Money remains a means for autonomy and travel, not the sole score. Revisit the dashboard quarterly, because a life is a trajectory, not a launch metric.

cards.name: A good life is more than a good feeling
cards.q: Boss fight, optional 15 min: write your operating philosophy for running MTRX for the next three years. Use at least one idea from each week of this guide. Make it operational: name two decisions it would change, one metric it would refuse to optimise, and one rule for what you do when money, growth and integrity conflict.
cards.answer: Model answer: I will run MTRX as a truth-seeking studio that makes useful work without pretending certainty. From Week 1, I will separate evidence from confidence and test claims with small pilots. From Week 2, I will remember that perception, memory and AI outputs are fallible, so I will show limits and keep call records. From Week 3, I will treat identity and social influence as pressures, not destiny, and build a team where dissent is safe. From Week 4, I will use Kant to refuse deceptive sustainability claims, Aristotle to practise honesty and courage until they are habits, existentialism to own choices made under constraint, and the good-life lens to protect writing, health, friendship and travel alongside revenue. I will change a decision when the evidence changes, but I will not optimise growth by making clients or staff less free. My dashboard will include profit, truthful client outcomes, creative hours, health and relationship time. A business that grows while training me to lie is a failed business, even if the monthly number rises.
